docs.html:
1Purpose

This policy sets out what [Provider name] commits to when a participant needs an injection under the skin. It is for participants, their families and advocates, our workers, and the people who check our work.

2Applies to

  • Every participant who needs a , in any setting: their own home, a shared home, respite, a centre or the community.
  • Every worker, contractor, agency worker and volunteer. Only a handles injecting equipment, sets a dose or gives an injection.
  • Every injectable medicine given by pen or pre-filled syringe, including insulin and blood thinners. A vial and syringe is covered only where the participant's plan names it.
  • Not covered: insulin pumps and other infusions, vaccines, injections into a vein or muscle, and controlled or cytotoxic medicines. This is our choice, narrower than the NDIS Commission's skills descriptor, which contemplates pumps; a provider may widen it under a separate plan as Ground rule 7 allows. Ground rule 7 says what happens instead.
  • This policy applies only while subcutaneous injections is set out in our certificate of registration (Practice Standards Rules, Schedule 2, clause 8(1)). If it is not, we do not take on the support and we help the participant find a provider who can.

A participant who gives their own injections with no help from us keeps doing so. Commitment 2 still applies to them.

3Commitments

C1

We will not let a worker give or help with an injection until the participant has a current plan from an appropriately qualified . The plan sets the medicine and device, how each dose is measured and any dose calculation, and the sites and their rotation. It also sets the readings and limits, the action for every band of reading, storage and sharps. A plan is current until its next review date. Where the review is late, a worker injects only while the , or the health practitioner who wrote the plan, has confirmed by phone or in writing, and we have recorded, that the plan stands pending the review.

Answers: Legislation (1). How we do it: Procedure step 2, Procedure step 3, Procedure step 12.

C2

We will make the plan with the participant, in their usual way of communicating. We record what they do themselves and how they want the injection done. We start from the participant giving their own injection if they want to. We respect a refusal, and never force, trick or hide an injection.

Answers: Legislation (1). How we do it: Procedure step 1, Procedure step 14.

C3

We will arrange a review of the participant's health status and plan, with their consent, by an appropriately qualified health practitioner. We do this at least every 12 months. We ask for an earlier review within 2 of a trigger listed in PRO-HID-07 Decision table 5, for example a hospital stay, a severe reaction or repeated calls to the health practitioner.

Answers: Legislation (1). How we do it: Procedure step 1, Procedure step 29.

C4

We will make sure the plan names, for each risk, what a worker does, whom they call, how fast, and when to call 000. The risks are a low or high reading, a wrong, missed or double dose, an allergic reaction, bleeding, a site reaction and a needlestick injury.

Answers: Legislation (1). How we do it: Procedure step 3, Procedure step 15, Procedure step 24.

C5

We will let a worker give an injection only under a current from the prescriber that matches the plan. If the order is unclear, out of date or does not match the plan, the worker does not give the dose and asks.

Answers: Legislation (2). How we do it: Procedure step 4, Procedure step 12.

C6

We will take a only where the medicines law of [state or territory] allows it, and only through an whom that law allows. Until the Quality Manager has recorded under Ground rule 4 the provision of that law that allows it, who may take it and the confirmation time it sets, we take no phone orders: every order comes in writing. Where phone orders are allowed, the order taker records the order, reads it back to the prescriber, and gets the prescriber's written confirmation within the time the law sets, and in any case within 24 hours. A phone order lapses if the confirmation is late. No phone order starts a medicine, changes a dose scale or a reading limit, or changes or stops insulin or a blood thinner. A phone order may hold a single dose.

Answers: Legislation (2). How we do it: Procedure step 9, Procedure step 10, Procedure step 11.

C7

We will limit each worker to the tasks the plan names and their sign-off lists. A trained worker may give a fixed dose from a pre-filled pen or syringe. They may read a written scale, or draw up from a vial, only where the plan names that task. Only the prescriber or the plan's health practitioner decides, changes or stops a dose.

Answers: Legislation (1), Legislation (3). How we do it: Procedure step 7, Procedure step 8, Procedure step 16.

C8

We will train each worker for this participant, this medicine and this device, and sign them off before their first unsupervised injection. A training plan names who needs which training and who delivers it. The trainer is an appropriately qualified health practitioner, or a person who meets the NDIS Commission's skills descriptor for subcutaneous injections. Each worker can explain the participant's related health condition in their own words.

Answers: Legislation (3), Legislation (4). How we do it: Procedure step 5, Procedure step 6, Procedure step 7.

C9

We will assess each worker again every 12 months. A sign-off lapses after 3 months without giving this participant's injection, and when the clinical content of the plan changes (a new review date or phone number does not lapse it); we assess again when it lapses, and after an error the worker's practice contributed to. A worker who is not assessed does not inject.

Answers: Legislation (4). How we do it: Procedure step 7, Procedure step 8.

C10

We will have a second person check independently every dose read from a scale or calculated, and every insulin or other high-risk dose where the plan says so. The plan names the for each shift and how they check: in person, by phone or by video. Where no second checker can be reached, the worker phones the before the dose, follows their instruction and records it.

Answers: Legislation (1). How we do it: Procedure step 8, Procedure step 19.

C11

We will keep each injectable labelled for one participant and stored as its label says. We will put every used needle and syringe straight into a at the point of use, and never recap. We treat a needlestick injury as an emergency: first aid, a medical review within 2 hours, and an incident report.

Answers: Legislation (3). How we do it: Procedure step 17, Procedure step 22, Procedure step 25.

C12

We will record every injection on the participant's medication administration record, with the site, the reading and the units given, and every refusal. We record each reading, scale line and second check on a blood glucose monitoring record. We keep these records for 7 years (NDIS Act 2013, section 45B, from 27 August 2026: records of claims and supports are kept for 7 years).

Answers: Legislation (3). How we do it: Procedure step 15, Procedure step 23.

C13

We will treat every injection error, near miss, reaction and needlestick injury as an incident. The worker gets health advice first. We tell the prescriber or health practitioner the same day. The Quality Manager, as the authorised notifier, decides whether the incident is reportable and notifies the NDIS Commission within 24 hours of becoming aware where the incident involves the death, serious injury, abuse or neglect, unlawful sexual or physical contact or sexual misconduct of a participant, or an unauthorised restrictive practice that resulted in harm; otherwise within 5 business days. We do not punish an honest report.

Answers: Legislation (3). How we do it: Procedure step 26, Procedure step 27.

C14

We will check each participant's injection records every week for completeness, and the will read a sample of each participant's records every month, and every record after an incident or a plan change. We audit injection practice every 6 months in the internal audit, with a desk review of the incident register and the weekly checks every 3 months. We give the governing body the trends and the improvements we recommend.

Answers: Legislation (3). How we do it: Procedure step 28, Procedure step 30.

4Ground rules

G1

The plan holds every clinical value for the participant: each dose, scale, reading limit, needle length, angle, site and dose time. This policy and its procedure hold none of them. Where our document and the plan differ on a value, the plan and the current order win.

G2

The plan cannot widen what a worker may do beyond PRO-HID-07 Decision table 3 and the worker's sign-off. A task that is not named is not allowed.

G3

For priming, air bubbles and in-use life, we follow the product information for the device in the plan. We do not teach or vary it.

G4

The medicines law of [state or territory] governs who may give an injection, who may take a phone order, controlled medicines and storage. Where it is stricter than this policy, the law applies. When we adopt this policy the Quality Manager records what it requires, including the provision that allows a phone order, who may take one and the confirmation time it sets, or records that it allows none. They check the record every 12 months. Until that record exists, every order comes in writing.

G5

An injection given mainly to influence a participant's behaviour is a . This policy authorises none. PRO-BSP-02 Regulated Restrictive Practices Procedure applies.

G6

If anything is unclear, the worker does not give the dose and asks. Asking is never an error.

G7

Pumps, infusions, vaccines, injections into a vein or muscle, and controlled and cytotoxic medicines are outside this policy. They stay with a nurse or other health practitioner. A worker takes part in a pump or an infusion only under a separate plan. The Clinical Lead and the participant's health practitioner write it, and name who does what.

G8

In a small provider one person may hold several roles. The Clinical Lead is a registered nurse, or another health practitioner whose scope covers the support, whom we engage to oversee high intensity supports. A sole trader cannot be their own Clinical Lead and engages one. A sole trader never signs off their own competency and never acts as their own second checker. They use the participant's pharmacist as the chart checker. A provider with no registered nurse takes no phone orders; every order comes in writing.

431 words
subcutaneous injection
an injection into the fat layer just under the skin, given with a pen, a pre-filled syringe, or a vial and syringe.
injection plan
the participant's plan for their injections, made with them and written by their health practitioner. It is held in FRM-HID-01 Participant Health Support Plan.
health practitioner
a registered practitioner whose scope covers the medicine, such as a medical practitioner, a nurse practitioner or a registered nurse. For insulin it can also be a credentialled diabetes educator who is also a registered health practitioner, working with the prescriber, who sets every dose and scale. A credentialled diabetes educator who holds no registration number is recorded by their ADEA credential and the prescriber co-signs the plan.
prescriber
the medical practitioner, nurse practitioner or other health practitioner who orders the medicine.
written order
the prescriber's signed and dated order. A secure message, fax or email from the practice counts as written.
phone order
an order the prescriber gives by phone or by word of mouth. It is recorded on FRM-HID-11 and confirmed in writing.
order taker
the registered nurse, or other person the medicines law of [state or territory] allows, who takes a phone order where Ground rule 4 allows one. A worker who is not an order taker never takes an order.
trained worker
a worker with a current sign-off for this participant, medicine and device in REG-HID-01.
second checker
the person the plan names to check a dose independently before it is given, in person, by phone or by video.
high-risk medicine
a medicine where a small mistake can cause serious harm, such as insulin or a blood thinner. The plan or the pharmacist says which of a participant's medicines are high-risk.
plan contact
the person or service the plan says to phone, in hours and after hours.
sharps container
a puncture-resistant container made for used needles and syringes.
Clinical Lead
a registered nurse, or another health practitioner whose scope covers the support, whom [Provider name] engages to oversee high intensity supports. A sole trader cannot be their own Clinical Lead and engages one.
on-call manager
the manager rostered to take calls at any hour. In office hours this is the Service Manager; after hours it is the rostered manager.
chemical restraint
the use of a medicine mainly to influence a person's behaviour. It does not include a medicine prescribed to treat a diagnosed mental disorder, a physical illness or a physical condition.
business day
a day other than a Saturday, a Sunday or a public holiday in the state or territory where the participant lives.

1Purpose

The result: each participant who needs an injection under the skin gets the right dose of the right medicine. A worker who is trained and signed off for them gives it, under a current plan and a current order. Every injection is recorded and every error is acted on.

This procedure gives effect to POL-HID-08 Subcutaneous Injections Policy, C1 to C14.

2When and who

Start this procedure when a participant needs a and wants our help with it. Use it before the first injection, at every injection, whenever an order or the plan changes, and whenever something goes wrong.

Where a Record line names a form or register that is not yet a Rise template, record the same facts in the participant's file under the same heading until it is. Where this procedure names an entry on the medication administration record (FRM-MED-01), it names the field in words; no question number of another provider's chart is used.

Who acts:

  • The Service Manager sets up the support, checks the plan and the orders, rosters workers, and checks the records every week.
  • The participant's writes and reviews the . The writes the orders. They may be the same person. They are usually not our workers.
  • The is a registered nurse, or another health practitioner whose scope covers the support, whom [Provider name] engages to oversee high intensity supports. They set the training plan, train and sign off workers, check the clinical items of each plan, read a monthly sample of records, give clinical advice and, when they are a registered nurse and POL-HID-08 Ground rule 4 allows it, may act as . Where PRO-MED-01 Management of Medication Procedure names a clinical adviser, that role is the Clinical Lead here when the adviser is a registered nurse.
  • The order taker is the only person who takes a , and only where POL-HID-08 Ground rule 4 records that the medicines law of [state or territory] allows it. It is a registered nurse, or another person that law allows.
  • The gives the injection, or helps the participant give it. A trained worker has a current sign-off for this participant, this medicine and this device in REG-HID-01 High Intensity Training and Competency Register.
  • The is the person the plan names to check a dose before it is given.
  • The is the person or service the plan says to phone, in hours and after hours.
  • The takes calls at any hour. In office hours this is the Service Manager.
  • The Quality Manager audits and reports, and, as the authorised notifier, decides whether an incident is reportable and notifies the NDIS Commission.

An injection incident is any error or near miss with an injection. It includes a wrong person, medicine, dose, device or time. It includes a missed or double dose, a dose given without the participant's agreement, a reaction, a spoiled medicine given, and any needlestick injury.

In a small provider one person may hold several roles. A sole trader holds them all, with three limits. They never sign off their own competency. They never act as their own second checker. They never take a phone order unless they are a registered nurse and POL-HID-08 Ground rule 4 allows it. A sole trader cannot be their own Clinical Lead and engages one, and asks the participant's pharmacist to be the chart checker. They name the second checker for every shift in each plan. Where a step says to phone the on-call manager, a sole trader phones the plan contact and writes down the time. A provider with no order taker, or whose Ground rule 4 record allows no phone orders, asks the prescriber to send every order in writing.

3Before you start

Trained workers:

  • Your name is in REG-HID-01 for this participant, this medicine and this device, and your sign-off has not expired.
  • You have read the participant's current plan. Its date is on the front, and its next review date has not passed.
  • You know the plan contact's numbers, the on-call number [on-call number], and who the second checker is on your shift.
  • You have the participant's own device and a new needle for each injection.
  • You have a within reach, and the meter and strips if the plan needs a reading.
  • You have the chart, clean hands and a private place the participant has agreed to.

The Service Manager, before the first injection:

  • You have the participant's agreement to the support and to health reviews (FRM-INF-01 Consent to Collect, Use and Share Information Form).
  • You know what the medicines law of [state or territory] requires. It covers who may give an injection, who may take a phone order, controlled medicines and storage. Where that law is stricter than this procedure, follow the law.
  • You hold the plan, and the plan holds every item below. If one is missing, send the plan back. No worker injects until it is complete.

What the plan must hold:

  • the participant's related health condition and what the medicine is for, in plain words
  • each medicine: name, strength, device, route, times, and the date of the order that covers it
  • how each dose is measured: the fixed dose in units, or the prescriber's written scale and how to read it
  • a statement that no worker changes a dose, a scale or a time without a new order
  • which tasks a worker may do: set the dose on a pen, read the written scale, draw up from a vial. Each task is named, or it is not allowed
  • who the second checker is on each shift, and how they check: in person, by phone or by video
  • needle length, angle, skin fold, holding time, injection sites and the order of rotation
  • each reading the plan needs, when, the limits for low, high and call 000, and the action for every band of reading, including a reading above the target range but below the call limit. A plan with a silent band is not complete
  • whether and when a ketone check is required, and the sick-day rules, where the practitioner sets any
  • for each risk, the action, the contact and the time limit. The risks are a wrong dose, a missed dose, a double dose, an allergic reaction, bleeding, a site reaction and a needlestick injury
  • how long to watch the participant after each dose
  • storage: the fridge range, in-use life, travel, and the stock check
  • the sharps container: who supplies it, and where it goes when full
  • what the participant does themselves, their wishes on privacy, timing, site and communication, and what helps them feel at ease
  • the health practitioner's name, profession and registration number, the plan date, the next review date, and the participant's consent to that review.

4Watch out

  • Call 000 first. Do this if the participant cannot be woken, cannot swallow safely or is fitting. Do it too for swelling of the face, lips or throat, trouble breathing, collapse or heavy bleeding. A severe allergic reaction can kill within minutes. A severe low can cause a fit or unconsciousness and needs 000 now.
  • A dose read wrongly from a scale is a wrong dose. A wrong dose of insulin can cause a severe low that lasts for hours. Never give a dose read from a scale or calculated, or an insulin dose the plan marks for a second check, without that check. If no second checker can be reached, phone the plan contact before the dose, follow their instruction and record it.
  • No reading, no dose, where the plan needs a reading. Insulin given without one can cause a severe low.
  • Never give an extra or catch-up dose. A double dose of insulin or a blood thinner can cause a severe low or serious bleeding.
  • One pen and one needle for one person. Sharing a pen, even with a new needle, can pass on a blood-borne infection.
  • Never recap a used syringe needle. A needlestick injury can pass on infection. Step 22 says how a pen needle comes off.
  • Heat and freezing spoil medicines. A spoiled injectable can look normal and still not work.
  • No means no. Forcing, tricking or hiding an injection takes away the participant's right to refuse. It can also be an unauthorised restrictive practice.
  • A phone order given to a worker is not an order. A misheard order is a wrong dose. Step 9 says what to do.
  • A signature before the injection is a false record. It hides a missed dose from the next worker and from the prescriber.

5Steps

Set up the support

Step 1

The Service Manager

Agree the support with the participant.

Start from the view that the participant gives their own injection if they want to. Ask what they do now, what help they want and how they like it done. Give them STA-HID-05 Subcutaneous Injections: Plain Summary, and go through it with them and a supporter they choose. Use their usual way of communicating. Ask if they agree to a health practitioner reviewing their health and plan, and to us sharing what we see with that practitioner. A guardian or other decision maker agrees only within the authority they hold. If the participant says no to either, write that down. Tell them that workers inject only under a current plan, and a plan needs its review. Offer to ask the health practitioner about other options, such as a community nurse. Never press. Ask who else should have a copy of the plan, such as family, another provider or a day service. Record their choice at FRM-INF-01.

Result
The participant has chosen the support, knows who does what, and has agreed to or declined the reviews.
Record
FRM-SUP-02; FRM-INF-01; REG-HID-02
Time limit
Before the first injection support (our standard)

Carries out: Policy C2, Policy C3.

Step 2

The Service Manager

Ask the participant's health practitioner to write the injection plan with the participant.

The health practitioner is a registered practitioner whose scope covers the medicine, such as a medical practitioner, a nurse practitioner or a registered nurse. For insulin it can also be a credentialled diabetes educator who is also a registered health practitioner, working with the prescriber. Check their registration on the national public register of health practitioners and write down the number. For a credentialled diabetes educator who holds no registration, record their ADEA credential and have the prescriber co-sign the plan. Send the participant's consent. Help the participant take part, in person or by video, with a supporter if they want one. Give the practitioner the list in "Before you start". The Clinical Lead may write the plan only if they are the appropriately qualified practitioner for this participant and medicine. Only the prescriber sets a dose or a scale. If the participant has no practitioner, the Clinical Lead helps them find one.

Result
A plan is being written with the participant by someone qualified to write it.

FRM-HID-01; REG-HID-02

Within 2 of the participant agreeing at step 1 (our standard)

Step 3

Warning. A plan with a missing limit, contact or review date can leave a worker with nothing to follow at 2 am.

The Service Manager for the administrative items, and the Clinical Lead for the clinical items

Check that the plan holds every item in "Before you start" and is the current plan.

Read the plan with the participant. The Service Manager checks the administrative items: the health practitioner has signed and dated it, the participant's part in it and their consent are written in it, the next review date is no more than 12 months after the plan date, and the contacts are complete. The Clinical Lead checks the clinical items: the dose and how it is measured, the needle length, angle, skin fold and holding time, the sites, the readings and limits, and that the plan states the action for every band of reading, including a reading above the target range but below the call limit. The Clinical Lead signs that check before the first dose. If an item is missing or a band is silent, send the plan back with the item named, and do not roster a worker to inject. When it is right, enter the plan date, the practitioner's name and registration number, the participant's consent and the next review date in REG-HID-02. Set a reminder 60 days before the review date. Where the plan needs a reading, attach the practitioner's own limits page as Section A of FRM-HID-12 where the plan has one; otherwise copy the limits onto Section A. The Clinical Lead checks that the attached page is the current plan's, or the copy against the plan, and signs it.

Workers have a complete plan with an instruction for every band, the review date is on record and watched, and the limits are in front of the worker.

Within 2 business days of receiving the plan, and before the first injection (our standard)

The Service Manager

Put each injectable on the chart from the prescriber's .

The Clinical Lead

Train in person, with the participant's own device or a demonstration device. Cover everything in the training plan. Let the worker practise each task while you watch. The Clinical Lead, or the health practitioner who wrote the plan

REG-HID-01

Every roster, before it is published (our standard)

Phone and verbal orders

Step 9

Warning. An order passed on by word of mouth can be misheard. A worker who is not an order taker has no authority to take one.

Any worker

If a prescriber, a nurse or anyone else phones or tells a worker an order, and the worker is not an order taker:

Say you cannot take an order, and take a message.

Say that you cannot take an order. Ask them to send it in writing, or say that our nurse will call back. Write down only the caller's name, practice and phone number. Add the time and the participant's name. Do not write down or act on any dose or medicine they say. Phone the on-call manager at once with the message. The on-call manager asks the order taker to call the prescriber back under step 10, or asks the prescriber to send the order in writing. If an order taker is on hand, pass the call to them. No worker acts on an unrecorded order, and the prescriber is called back by someone who may take the order.

FRM-SUP-08

Step 10

Warning. A phone order has no written copy to check. A misheard dose or unit can reach the participant before anyone sees it.

The order taker

Take the phone order on FRM-HID-11.

Take a phone order only where POL-HID-08 Ground rule 4 records that the medicines law of [state or territory] allows you to; otherwise tell the prescriber, ask for a written order and stop. Call the prescriber back on the practice number in the participant's file, never on a number the caller gave you. Hand the record to the Service Manager, or to the on-call manager after hours, who names the trained workers who may give it, and say which dose is due next.

The order is written in full, read back and confirmed, and its written confirmation is due.

FRM-HID-11 Q1 to Q24

During the call. Written confirmation due within the time the medicines law of [state or territory] sets, and in any case within 24 hours of the call (our standard)

Ask their name and date of birth. If they cannot tell you, use the photo and one other identifier on the chart. Do this every time, even when you know them well. If you cannot be sure, do not inject. Phone the on-call manager.

The injection is about to go to the right person.

Before each injection (our standard)

The trained worker

Ask the participant if they want the injection now.

Use their usual way of communicating. Say which medicine it is and what it is for. Agree a private place, and agree who does which part. Ask what helps them feel at ease. The plan lists what the participant does themselves, for example dialling the pen or choosing the site. If they say no, or show no, accept it. Do not persuade, hurry, bribe or trick. Before each injection (our standard)

Let the participant take it if they want to. Wash your hands. Use the participant's own meter. Check the strips are in date and the meter shows no error. Check what the plan says about the meal. You know the reading and what the plan says to do about it.

If the plan says the dose comes from a written scale:

Read the dose, in units, from the plan's written scale.

The trained worker

The second checker

If the dose is read from a scale or calculated, or it is insulin or another medicine the plan marks high-risk and the plan says it needs a second check:

Check the dose independently before it is given.

The trained worker tells you the participant's name and date of birth, the medicine, the reading and the scale line if there is one. They show or read out what the device is set to. Before the injection (our standard)

The trained worker

Choose the site with the participant, and check the skin.

Use the next site on the plan's rotation. Ask the participant if they want a different site from the list. Help them into the position the plan names, in private. Look at the skin. Give the injection as the plan and the product information say.

The plan sets the needle length, angle, skin fold and holding time. Follow it. Where the plan is silent on holding time, use the product information. Tell the participant before you touch them. The participant does any part the plan lists for them. Watch the participant's face and breathing while you inject. Hold the device in place for the holding time, then take it out. Warning. A used needle can injure the next person and pass on infection. Never recap a used syringe needle, and never bend or break any needle.

Put the used needle or syringe into the sharps container at once.

The pen stays with the participant. Never pass a used needle hand to hand. Never put a sharp in a bin, a bag or a cup. Between injections, keep the container closed, upright and out of reach of children and visitors. Close it for good at the fill line and tell the Service Manager. They replace it and arrange disposal under PRO-WST-01 Management of Waste Procedure and the sharps rules of [state or territory]. If anyone is stuck by a used needle, go now to Decision table 4. Use the row that starts "A used needle has pricked or cut anyone".

Result
No used needle or syringe is left out, and the container is safe.
Record
None
Time limit
Straight away, at the point of use (our standard)

Carries out: Policy C11.

Step 23

The trained worker

Sign the chart with the code, the time, the reading, the units and the site.

Enter the code for "given" if you gave it, and the code for "self-administered with help" if the participant gave it with your help. In the notes, write the reading, the units given, the site used, and the second checker's name where one was needed. Add anything unusual. Sign only for a dose you gave or saw given. Never sign before the dose, for another worker, or from memory at the end of the shift.

Result
The chart shows what was given, where, when and by whom.
Record
FRM-MED-01 (the administration entry: date, time, code, signature and notes)
Time limit
Straight after the injection (our standard)

Carries out: Policy C12.

Step 24

Warning. A severe reaction or a low can start within minutes of an injection.

The trained worker

Watch the participant for the effects and reactions the plan lists.

Stay for the time the plan sets, then keep watching for the rest of your shift. Ask how they feel and look at the site. Look for the signs of a low, a high, an allergic reaction, bleeding and a site reaction. Look for the medicine's side effects. The plan lists each one. Call 000 if the participant cannot be woken, cannot swallow safely or is fitting. Call 000 for swelling of the face or throat, trouble breathing, collapse or heavy bleeding. For anything else, follow Decision table 4 and phone the plan contact. At the end of your shift hand over to the next worker any reading outside the limits, held dose, reaction or advice you were given. If the plan is not meeting the participant's needs, or they ask for a change, tell the Service Manager the same shift.

Result
A reaction or a low is noticed at once and passed on.
Record
FRM-MED-01 (the observation note); FRM-SUP-08
Time limit
The time the plan sets, then the rest of your shift (the plan; our standard)

Carries out: Policy C4.

Step 25

The trained worker

Put the medicine and equipment away as the label and the plan say.

Unopened pens and syringes stay in the fridge at the range on the label. A pen in use is kept as the product information says. Label it with the participant's name, the date opened and the discard date. Never freeze it. Never leave it in a vehicle or in the sun. For an outing, carry it in its case as the plan says. At the start of each shift where we hold the medicine, read the fridge thermometer. If it is outside the range, do not use the cold medicines. Phone the pharmacist and the on-call manager. Tell the Service Manager if pens, needles, strips or the sharps container will run out within 7 days.

Result
The medicine is safe for the next dose and nothing will run out unnoticed.
Record
FRM-MED-01 (the fridge temperature entry)
Time limit
Straight after each injection. The fridge check at the start of each shift (our standard)

Carries out: Policy C11.

Report and check

Step 26

The trained worker, or any worker who sees it

If an injection incident has happened, or a refused or missed dose of insulin or a blood thinner:

Report the injection incident to the on-call manager and write the incident report.

Make the participant safe first. Decision table 4 says what to do and whom to call. Then phone the on-call manager as soon as the participant is safe. Write Sections A to D of the incident report and choose "medication" as the kind of incident. Choose "other injury" for a needlestick. Report a near miss the same way. Report your own error. We do not punish an honest report. PRO-INC-01 Incident Management Procedure then applies from step 8. The Quality Manager, as the authorised notifier, decides whether the incident is reportable and notifies the NDIS Commission.

Result
A manager has taken charge and the incident is on record while memory is fresh.
Record
FRM-INC-01 Sections A to D; FRM-MED-01 (the administration entry notes); FRM-HID-12 Q27
Time limit
Phone as soon as the participant is safe. Write the report before your shift ends (our standard). For a reportable incident the law says as soon as possible (statutory: Incident Management and Reportable Incidents Rules, section 19)

Carries out: Policy C13. Written on: FRM-HID-12 Q24, FRM-HID-12 Q25, FRM-HID-12 Q26, FRM-HID-12 Q27.

Step 27

The on-call manager, or the Service Manager in office hours

Tell the prescriber or the health practitioner about the injection incident, and ask for their advice.

Phone the plan contact. Say what happened, what the participant's readings and signs were, and what was done. Ask if the plan, the order or the next doses need to change, and if the participant needs an early review under Decision table 5. Write who you told, when, and their advice. Tell the participant honestly what happened, in their usual way of communicating. Where the incident is reportable, PRO-INC-02 Reportable Incidents Notification Procedure applies. The Quality Manager, as the authorised notifier, notifies the NDIS Commission within 24 hours of becoming aware where the incident involves the death, serious injury, abuse or neglect, unlawful sexual or physical contact or sexual misconduct of a participant, or an unauthorised restrictive practice that resulted in harm; otherwise within 5 business days.

Result
The prescriber knows, the advice is on record, and the participant has been told.
Record
FRM-INC-01 (prescriber told); REG-INC-01 (prescriber or practitioner told, date and advice)
Time limit
The same day (our standard). Notifying the Commission: within 24 hours of becoming aware where the incident involves the death, serious injury, abuse or neglect, unlawful sexual or physical contact or sexual misconduct of a participant, or an unauthorised restrictive practice that resulted in harm; otherwise within 5 business days (statutory: Incident Management and Reportable Incidents Rules, sections 20 and 21)

Carries out: Policy C13.

Step 28

The Service Manager

Check every participant's injection records.

Where the Service Manager gave the injections, another manager or the Clinical Lead does this check. Read each entry since the last check in FRM-MED-01 and FRM-HID-12. Look for empty boxes and a reading outside the limits with no action. Look for a call limit reached with no call, a band the plan is silent on, and a dose read from a scale or calculated, or an insulin dose the plan marks for a second check, with no second check. Look for the same site used twice in a row against the rotation, and a phone order with no confirmation by its due time. Look for a plan or a sign-off that will expire within 60 days, a sharps container near full, and low stock. Count the calls to the plan contact. Three or more for the same reason in 7 days is a trigger in Decision table 5. Raise an incident report for any error nobody reported. Put an action that will take more than 7 days in REG-QMS-01 Continuous Improvement Register. The Clinical Lead reads a sample of each participant's records every month, and every record after an incident or a plan change, and raises any clinical concern with the plan contact.

Result
Gaps are found and fixed within a week.
Record
FRM-HID-12 Q28; REG-QMS-01
Time limit
The Service Manager every 7 days. The Clinical Lead every month, and within 1 week of an incident or a plan change (our standard)

Carries out: Policy C14. Written on: FRM-HID-12 Q28.

Step 29

The Service Manager

Ask the health practitioner to review the participant's health and plan.

Do this with the participant's consent from step 1. Ask at least 60 days before the review date in REG-HID-02. That date is never more than 12 months after the plan date. Ask within 2 business days of any trigger in Decision table 5. Send what the records show: readings outside the limits, calls, refusals, incidents and site problems. Help the participant attend. After the review, enter the date, the practitioner, the outcome and the next review date in REG-HID-02. If the plan changed, repeat steps 3 to 5 for the changed parts. Assess each worker again under step 7. No worker injects on the new plan until they are briefed. Give the new plan to the people the participant chose at step 1. If the review cannot happen before the review date, ask the practitioner for a written extension with a new date. A plan with no review and no extension is out of date.

Result
A qualified practitioner has reviewed the participant's health and plan, and the review dates are on record.
Record
REG-HID-02; FRM-HID-12 Q29
Time limit
A review at least every 12 months, asked for 60 days ahead. A request within 2 business days of a trigger (our standard)

Carries out: Policy C3. Written on: FRM-HID-12 Q29.

Step 30

The Quality Manager

Audit injection practice.

Sample participants who have injections. For each, check the plan is current and complete, and the order on the chart matches it. Check each phone order has its confirmation in time, and each worker's sign-off in REG-HID-01 is current. Check second checks are recorded, and storage and the sharps container are right, seen in person. Ask two trained workers what the participant's condition is, what a low looks like for them, and what they would do. Count injection incidents in REG-INC-01 Incident Register by type, cause, place and time of day. Report the results and trends to the governing body, with the improvements you recommend. Put each action in REG-QMS-01. Take lessons, with names removed, to team meetings. A sole trader engages the Clinical Lead to do this audit.

Result
Patterns are seen and acted on before they harm someone.
Record
REG-QMS-02 Internal Audit Schedule and Register; REG-QMS-01
Time limit
Every 6 months, in the internal audit. A desk review of REG-INC-01 and the weekly checks every 3 months (our standard)

Carries out: Policy C14.

  • each injection due has been given as planned, or the record shows why not and who was told
  • every used needle and syringe is in the sharps container, and the medicine is stored right
  • every injection incident has an incident report and a row in REG-INC-01 Incident Register.

form.intro:
This record holds one medication order that a prescriber gives by phone or by word of mouth, for a participant who has . Only an order taker completes it, and only where POL-HID-08 Subcutaneous Injections Policy Ground rule 4 records that the medicines law of [state or territory] allows a phone order. A worker who is not an order taker never takes an order and never acts on one. PRO-HID-07 Subcutaneous Injections Procedure, step 9, says what a worker does when a prescriber calls.

Who completes it, and when:

  • Sections A to E: the order taker, during the call. Take questions 6, 10, 11, 12, 14, 21 and 22 first, while the prescriber is on the line; complete the rest from the chart straight after the call. Questions 19 and 20 are the Service Manager's.
  • Section F: the order taker sets the due time during the call. The Service Manager completes the rest when the written confirmation arrives.
  • Section G, and questions 19 and 20: the Service Manager, before the next dose of the medicine is due.

Have ready: the participant's chart (FRM-MED-01) and plan (FRM-HID-01), the practice's phone number from the participant's file, and a pen. If a second listener is near, ask them to listen.

Storage, self-management and general consent belong in the participant's medication plan (FRM-MED-02) and the participant's support plan, not here.

What happens next: the Service Manager puts the order on the chart, tells the participant and briefs the trained workers. The Service Manager then checks the prescriber's written confirmation. The record is filed with the chart.

Every copy of this record carries these lines:

  • A worker who is not an order taker and is phoned an order takes a message only. The worker does not write down or act on the order.
  • A phone order cannot start a medicine, change a dose scale or a reading limit, or change insulin or a blood thinner. PRO-HID-07 Decision table 1 lists what a phone order can and cannot do.
  • The prescriber's written confirmation is due within the time the medicines law of [state or territory] sets, and in any case within 24 hours of the call. If it is late, the order has lapsed and no worker gives a dose from it.
  • If you cannot read the order back to the prescriber, do not accept it.
  • This record is used only where the Quality Manager has recorded, under POL-HID-08 Ground rule 4, the provision of the medicines law of [state or territory] that allows the order taker to take a phone order: [provision, recorded at adoption]. Where no provision is recorded, every order comes in writing.
form.privacy:
This record holds health information about the participant. We collect it so that a phone order is written down in full, read back, confirmed in writing and acted on safely. It also shows who said what and when.

The order taker, the Service Manager, the trained workers named at question 19, the and the Quality Manager read it. With the participant's consent we share it with their prescriber, their pharmacist and other health services. In an emergency we give it to ambulance or hospital staff where the law allows. FRM-INF-01 Consent to Collect, Use and Share Information Form records the consent.

If you are the participant, you can ask to see this record and ask us to correct it. POL-INF-01 Information Management Policy sets how we store and protect it.

The record also holds the names, roles and phone numbers of the prescriber and the order taker. We keep them so the order can be traced to the people who gave and took it.
form.after:
• Order taker: give the completed record to the Service Manager, or to the after hours, straight after the read-back. Say which dose is due next (our standard).
  • Service Manager: put the order on the chart, tell the participant and brief the trained workers. Do this before the next dose of that medicine is due (our standard). PRO-HID-07 step 4 sets how.
  • Service Manager: check the written confirmation as soon as it arrives, and again at the due time (our standard). PRO-HID-07 step 11 sets how.
  • Service Manager: file the record with the chart in the participant's file within 7 days of the confirmation check (our standard).
  • Quality Manager: sample these records in the 3 month desk review and the 6 month injection audit under PRO-HID-07 step 30.
  • Keep each record for 7 years after its last entry (NDIS Act 2013, section 45B, from 27 August 2026: records of claims and supports are kept for 7 years). The health records law of [state or territory] can require longer, and so can a record about a child.

form.intro:
This record holds each blood glucose reading for one participant. It sets each reading against the limits their health practitioner wrote in their plan, and says what was done about it. It also holds each dose worked out from a written scale, with its second check. Use one record for each participant and each plan. Start a new one when the plan changes.

Who completes it, and when:

  • Section A: the Service Manager attaches the practitioner's own limits page where the plan has one, or copies the limits from the plan once. The Clinical Lead or the health practitioner checks it, and checks that the plan gives an instruction for every band of reading, before anyone uses it.
  • Sections B and C: the at each reading and each dose, answering only the questions the list below sets for that use. The participant may take their own reading and say the number. The worker still writes it.
  • Section D: the trained worker, whenever a reading is outside the limits, the plan is silent for the band, a dose is held or a call is made.
  • Section E: the Service Manager every week. The Clinical Lead reads a sample every month, and every record after an incident or a plan change.

Have ready: the plan (FRM-HID-01), the order on the chart (FRM-MED-01), and the participant's own meter and strips. Have the written scale too if the plan uses one. Never copy a scale onto this record. Read it from the plan.

What happens next: the Service Manager reads this record every week and checks the pattern. A page is filed in the participant's file when it is full.

When, and which questions to complete:

  • A routine reading inside the target range with no dose due: questions 12 to 18.
  • A reading before an insulin or other high-risk dose: questions 12 to 18, then 22 and 23 where the plan requires a second check.
  • A dose read from a scale: questions 12 to 23.
  • A reading below the low limit, at or above the call limit or in a band the plan is silent on, a held dose, or any call: also questions 24 to 27.
  • Questions 1 to 11 are completed once per page.

Every page of this record shows the practitioner who set the limits, the limits themselves, and who to call (Section A). It also carries these lines:

  • Cannot be woken, cannot swallow safely, fitting, trouble breathing or swelling of the face or throat: call 000 now.
  • No reading, no dose, where the plan needs a reading.
  • A reading below the low limit, or at or above the call limit: stop and follow the plan. If the plan gives no instruction for the band you are in, phone the plan contact before the dose. Never guess a dose and never change one.
form.privacy:
This record holds health information about the participant. We collect it so that workers give the right dose at the right time and act on a low or a high reading. It also shows the health practitioner what happened between reviews.

The trained workers, the second checkers, the Service Manager, the Clinical Lead and the Quality Manager read it. With the participant's consent we share it with their health practitioner, their and other health services. In an emergency we give it to ambulance or hospital staff where the law allows. FRM-INF-01 Consent to Collect, Use and Share Information Form records the consent.

If you are the participant, you can ask to see this record and ask us to correct it. POL-INF-01 Information Management Policy sets how we store and protect it.
form.after:
• Trained worker: hand over any reading outside the limits, held dose or call to the next worker before your shift ends (our standard).
  • Trained worker: phone the on-call manager about any reading that needed a call to the plan contact or 000, before your shift ends (our standard).
  • Service Manager: read the record every week and complete question 28 (our standard). Clinical Lead: read a sample every month, and every record after an incident or a plan change (our standard).
  • Service Manager: send a summary to the health practitioner at each review, and within 2 when question 29 shows a trigger (our standard).
  • Service Manager: file each full page in the participant's file within 7 days of its last entry (our standard).
  • Quality Manager: sample these records in the 3 month desk review and the 6 month injection audit under PRO-HID-07 step 30.
  • Keep each page for 7 years after its last entry (NDIS Act 2013, section 45B, from 27 August 2026: records of claims and supports are kept for 7 years). The health records law of [state or territory] can require longer, and so can a record about a child.
  • A page that records an incident is kept with the incident record for the time REG-INC-01 Incident Register sets.
